screens.title: Open/Closed Principle — Open for Extension, Closed for Modification
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore the Open/Closed Principle, a cornerstone of building stable, maintainable systems. The principle says that once a software entity works, you should avoid changing its existing code to add new behaviors; instead, you extend it. That sounds paradoxical at first — how can something be both open and closed? The resolution is abstraction: design modules to depend on contracts, then add new implementations behind those contracts. This reduces regression risk, localizes change, and makes systems easier to test. You will see common violations that emerge as sprawling conditional logic and learn practical refactoring steps to convert those into extension points. We'll walk through concrete examples — a PaymentProcessor full of if-else branches and a DiscountCalculator used in a hands-on activity — and show how introducing interfaces or small strategy classes removes the need to modify stable code. By the end, you'll be able to recognize OCP violations, decide when to add an abstraction, and apply safe refactorings that keep your codebase predictable. Consider this question as we begin: where in your current projects have you repeatedly changed the same function to add new behavior?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Open/Closed Principle
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Open/Closed Principle

Learn why well-designed code should accept new behaviors by extension rather than by changing tested implementations, and how abstraction solves the apparent paradox.

In this lesson

You will identify OCP violations, follow a safe refactoring path, and apply interfaces to keep code stable while adding features.

Coming up

Real examples: PaymentProcessor and DiscountCalculator. Practical refactor: conditional logic -> interface implementations.

Explore Key Topics
The Paradox
Understand what 'open' and 'closed' actually refer to and how abstraction reconciles them.
Common Violations
Spot if-else/switch hotspots that force edits when new types arrive.
Refactoring Path
A stepwise approach: extract interface, add implementations, inject dependencies.
Stable Core
Untouched business logic
Abstraction
An interface or abstract class that contracts behavior
New Implementations
Add concrete types without editing the core
Safer Changes
Fewer regressions, easier testing
Visual analogy: a stable chassis with plug-in modules

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will be able to define the Open/Closed Principle precisely, explain the apparent paradox, and identify real code smells that violate it. First, you'll learn the formal definition: software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. That means you can add new behaviors without changing the code that already works. Second, you'll see how abstraction — interfaces or abstract classes — resolves the paradox by making the parts that vary replaceable. Third, you'll recognize common violations, especially large conditional blocks that require edits whenever a new type is added. Finally, you'll appreciate why OCP matters: it reduces the risk of regressions, simplifies maintenance, and supports reuse. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters. As you study examples and refactorings in this lesson, check which objectives you can demonstrate by writing a small interface and replacing conditionals with new implementations. Keep a mental note of one place in your codebase where this approach could reduce future edits.

screens.title: What OCP Actually Means
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the Open/Closed Principle in practical terms. The claim is simple: you should be able to add new functionality to a module without editing its existing, tested source code. That avoids introducing regressions into behavior you rely on. The apparent paradox — being both open and closed — is resolved when you separate what varies from what stays the same. The part that stays the same becomes closed or stable; the part that varies is represented by an abstraction that can be extended. For example, instead of a single class with many internal branches, define an interface that describes the operation you need. Then provide concrete implementations for each behavior. This way you add a new class when requirements change, rather than editing the original class. A common misconception is that OCP forbids all changes. It doesn't. Bug fixes and adjustments of the core are still modifications. OCP specifically guides how to add new behaviors without touching the proven core. Practically, this reduces regression risk, improves testability because each implementation can be tested in isolation, and makes the system easier to reason about. Think about one conditional you maintain often; could that be an interface with two or three implementations instead?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › What OCP Actually Means
Core idea

Open for extension: accept new concrete behaviors. Closed for modification: avoid changing code that already works. Abstraction is the bridge.

Analogy
Think of a chassis you never change; new modules plug into it. The chassis is closed; modules are open.
Common misconception
OCP is not 'never change code'. It prescribes how to add new feature behavior, not to block bug fixes.
Key Takeaway

Separate stable logic from variable behavior by introducing abstractions you can extend.

How abstraction resolves the paradox
Define a contract
Create an interface describing the operation you need, not the concrete steps.
Provide implementations
Each concrete behavior becomes its own class implementing that contract.
Plug without changing
The original client uses the abstraction; adding a new implementation requires no edits to the client.
Example prompt
Look for a function you edit often to add cases. Could it be an interface with implementations instead?

screens.title: Open for Extension vs Closed for Modification
screens.narratorSegment: It's useful to separate the two halves of the principle and see their consequences. 'Open for extension' means you can add new behavior without changing the existing code base. This supports adding features by introducing new classes or modules that implement a common contract. 'Closed for modification' means once a component is established and tested, you minimize edits to its source to avoid regressions. Together they mean design for change rather than making change in place. Practically, open-for-extension encourages small, focused implementations: each new behavior is its own unit. Closed-for-modification pushes you to keep the core A P I stable and to let new behaviors plug in. A common mistake is to satisfy open-for-extension by duplicating or branching inside the same class, which violates closed-for-modification. Another misconception is to rigidly avoid refactoring; in reality, refactoring is how you achieve OCP — you extract abstractions and move behavior out. Consider this scenario: a reporting module grows formats. If you keep editing the big switch statement, you violate closed-for-modification. If instead you introduce a Report interface and add PDF, CSV, and Excel implementations, you stay closed to modification and open to extension. What would you extract first when you see a growing switch statement?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Open vs Closed
Open for extension

Add new behaviors by creating new implementations of an abstraction rather than editing existing code.

Example
Create new payment method classes instead of changing the processor each time.
Benefit
Easier testing and isolated feature changes.
Closed for modification

Preserve the existing implementation to avoid introducing regressions; add features by adding new code instead.

Common violation
Long if-else or switch blocks that are updated each time a new type is required.
Practical tip
Extract the varying behavior into a small interface and replace branches with polymorphism.

screens.title: PaymentProcessor with Conditional Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine a concrete code example that violates OCP and practice stating exactly why it does so. The PaymentProcessor class accepts a payment type string and uses an if-else cascade to choose behavior. Each time a new payment method arrives, you must open and edit the existing method to add another branch. That is changing working code to add new features, which increases regression risk. The code works for the current set of payment types, but it is brittle because every addition requires modification. A better design introduces a PaymentMethod abstraction that the processor depends on. Then new payment types are new classes implementing that abstraction and the processor simply calls a single method on the contract. A common misconception is that conditionals are harmless when small. They are harmless short-term, but once they grow and are edited repeatedly, they become maintenance hotspots. As you read the code, ask: who owns the decision logic? If the processor does, we violate OCP; if an injected strategy does, we comply. Consider how you would change the current class to add ApplePay. Would you edit the method or add a new class?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › PaymentProcessor — Violation
Problem code (simplified)
public class PaymentProcessor {
    public void processPayment(String paymentType, double amount) {
        if ("CreditCard".equals(paymentType)) {
            processCreditCardPayment(amount);
        } else if ("PayPal".equals(paymentType)) {
            processPayPalPayment(amount);
        } else if ("BankTransfer".equals(paymentType)) {
            processBankTransferPayment(amount);
        } else {
            System.out.println("Unsupported payment type: " + paymentType);
        }
    }

    private void processCreditCardPayment(double amount) { /* ... */ }
    private void processPayPalPayment(double amount) { /* ... */ }
    private void processBankTransferPayment(double amount) { /* ... */ }
}
Explanation
  • Each new payment method requires editing processPayment and adding a branch.
  • Edit of existing, tested code increases regression risk and maintenance cost.
  • A single responsibility is blurred: the processor decides which concrete behavior to run.
Concrete idea
Introduce a PaymentMethod interface and let the processor call a single process method on it.
Key Takeaway

When adding types forces edits to a method, extract an abstraction and add implementations instead.

screens.title: Step-by-step: From Conditional to OCP
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring a conditional hotspot into an OCP-compliant design is best done in small, verifiable steps. First, identify the smallest unit of varying behavior in your conditional. Second, extract an interface that captures that behavior with a single method name and clear inputs. Third, create concrete implementations for each existing branch and make sure their behavior matches current behavior. Fourth, update the original client to depend on the abstraction and accept implementations, for example by constructor injection or a registry lookup. Fifth, add tests for each implementation and for the client using a mock abstraction to ensure behavior remains unchanged. Finally, remove the old conditional only once tests confirm equivalence. Each step reduces risk: you never leave the system in an untested, broken state. A common misconception is that this must be done in a single big rewrite. Instead, move one branch at a time: extract one implementation, wire it in, test, then proceed. Following this incremental path keeps the codebase stable and makes code review simpler, because each change is small and focused. Step-by-step: From Conditional to OCP means extract an interface, implement behaviors, inject the abstraction, and remove the conditional only after tests validate behavior.. In practical terms, a safe refactoring path you can apply incrementally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Refactoring Process
Incremental steps
  1. Identify variation: find the single responsibility that changes between branches.
  2. Define interface: declare a concise contract with one clear method.
  3. Implement one by one: move an existing branch into a new class and run tests.
  4. Inject abstraction: change the client to accept the abstraction rather than make decisions.
  5. Test and remove: ensure behavior parity then remove the conditional safely.
Concrete example
For PaymentProcessor: extract PaymentMethod interface, add CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment classes, and inject appropriate implementation.
Why tests matter
Tests verify each implementation and the client behavior so you can remove the conditional with confidence.
Common mistake
Extracting interfaces prematurely for speculative features; prefer incremental extraction for likely changes.
Key Takeaway

Refactor stepwise, test each change, and only remove conditionals when behavior is covered by tests.

screens.title: Depend on Abstractions: Interface-Based Design
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable way to achieve OCP is to have high-level clients depend on abstractions rather than concrete classes. The PaymentProcessor should not know the details of each payment method; it should call a single method defined by an interface. This reverses the decision responsibility: concrete implementations decide how to perform the operation, while the processor coordinates. In architecture terms, place the abstraction between the stable core and the variable implementations. The core exposes a small, stable interface. Implementations live behind that interface and can be added freely. In practice you can provide implementations via constructor injection, a factory, or a registry. Each approach has trade-offs: constructor injection is explicit and testable, a factory centralizes creation, and a registry can support runtime lookup. A misconception is that interfaces add too much ceremony; when well-scoped they simplify reasoning and testing. As a practical exercise, design a PaymentMethod interface with a single process method, then implement CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment. The processor's code remains unchanged when you add an ApplePay implementation later. Depend on Abstractions: Interface-Based Design means place an abstraction between core logic and variable implementations; depend on the abstraction to accept new behaviors.. In practical terms, how a client uses an abstraction to remain closed while accepting extensions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity centers on a DiscountCalculator that uses customer type strings and a chain of conditionals to compute discounts. Run the starter code and then imagine adding a new 'Loyalty' customer type with a 12 percent discount. To support this new type with the current implementation, you would edit the calculateDiscount method and add another else-if branch. Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › DiscountCalculator Activity
Starter code (simplified)
public class DiscountCalculator {
    public double calculateDiscount(String customerType, double purchaseAmount) {
        double discount = 0;

        if ("Standard".equalsIgnoreCase(customerType)) {
            discount = purchaseAmount * 0.05;
            System.out.println("Applying Standard discount.");
        } else if ("Premium".equalsIgnoreCase(customerType)) {
            discount = purchaseAmount * 0.10;
            System.out.println("Applying Premium discount.");
        } else if ("VIP".equalsIgnoreCase(customerType)) {
            discount = purchaseAmount * 0.15;
            System.out.println("Applying VIP discount.");
        } else {
            System.out.println("No specific discount for customer type: " + customerType);
        }
        return discount;
    }
}
Activity steps
  • Run the main class to observe current outputs for Standard, Premium, and VIP.
  • Imagine adding Loyalty with a 12% rate — note you must edit calculateDiscount to add a branch.
  • Plan an extraction: define DiscountStrategy.calculate, implement classes for each type, and let the calculator select the strategy.
Why this matters
A new class for Loyalty keeps existing code unchanged and reduces risk of breaking other discount logic.
Key Takeaway

Use strategy-like abstractions to add customer types without changing the calculator's core logic.

screens.title: Avoiding Over-Engineering
screens.narratorSegment: Applying OCP requires judgment. Introducing an interface for every tiny variation leads to unnecessary complexity and cognitive overhead. The rule of thumb is to anticipate likely changes and avoid speculative abstractions. Ask: how often will this behavior change, and who will maintain the new code? If a conditional is unlikely to change or covers an ephemeral requirement, keep it simple. If a conditional occurs in multiple places or is edited frequently, extract an abstraction. A common mistake is to extract too-general interfaces that try to cover many unrelated cases; those become brittle and defeat the purpose of modularity. Balance is the goal: use OCP where it reduces repeated edits and simplifies maintenance, and avoid it when it adds speculative layers with little immediate benefit. screens.title: How OCP Improves Testing and Reduces Regressions
screens.narratorSegment: OCP directly improves testability and system stability. When behavior is implemented in small, focused classes behind an interface, each implementation can be unit-tested in isolation. The client can be tested with a mock or stub of the abstraction, ensuring its orchestration logic remains correct. This separation reduces the blast radius of changes: adding a new implementation doesn't alter the client's code, so existing tests continue to validate the core. Consider a PaymentProcessor that depends on a PaymentMethod interface. You can test the processor using a fake implementation that records calls without invoking external APIs. You can test each concrete payment class for correctness and side effects with integration tests. A common misunderstanding is that OCP increases test surface; in fact, it localizes tests to small units and keeps the contract between them explicit. In practice this makes diagnosing regressions faster because tests failing are likely localized to a single implementation rather than spread across a monolithic conditional. screens.title: Mistakes, Misconceptions, and Allowed Modifications
screens.narratorSegment: Developers often misunderstand OCP in three main ways. First, some think OCP means never change any code. That is incorrect. Bug fixes, performance improvements, and necessary corrective edits are allowed. OCP specifically discourages changing working code to add new behaviors. Second, teams sometimes over-apply OCP and create abstractions for every anticipated possibility, leading to needless complexity. The balance is to design for likely changes and keep interfaces small. Third, many people conflate single responsibility with OCP; although related, SRP is about having one reason to change a class, while OCP is about how to add new behaviors without modifying existing code. Common mistakes in code are duplicating conditional logic across modules, or hiding variation behind ad-hoc string keys and registries without clear contracts. When you refactor, prioritize test coverage so that edits and extractions do not accidentally change behavior. Finally, remember that OCP is a design guideline to reduce risk and aid maintainability — apply it pragmatically, not dogmatically. End with a reflective question: which recurring edit in your codebase would benefit most from an interface extraction? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore the Open/Closed Principle, a cornerstone of building stable, maintainable systems. The principle says that once a software entity works, you should avoid changing its existing code to add new behaviors; instead, you extend it. That sounds paradoxical at first — how can something be both open and closed? The resolution is abstraction: design modules to depend on contracts, then add new implementations behind those contracts. This reduces regression risk, localizes change, and makes systems easier to test. You will see common violations that emerge as sprawling conditional logic and learn practical refactoring steps to convert those into extension points. We'll walk through concrete examples — a PaymentProcessor full of if-else branches and a DiscountCalculator used in a hands-on activity — and show how introducing interfaces or small strategy classes removes the need to modify stable code. By the end, you'll be able to recognize OCP violations, decide when to add an abstraction, and apply safe refactorings that keep your codebase predictable. Consider this question as we begin: where in your current projects have you repeatedly changed the same function to add new behavior?

By the end of these screens you will be able to define the Open/Closed Principle precisely, explain the apparent paradox, and identify real code smells that violate it. First, you'll learn the formal definition: software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. That means you can add new behaviors without changing the code that already works. Second, you'll see how abstraction — interfaces or abstract classes — resolves the paradox by making the parts that vary replaceable. Third, you'll recognize common violations, especially large conditional blocks that require edits whenever a new type is added. Finally, you'll appreciate why OCP matters: it reduces the risk of regressions, simplifies maintenance, and supports reuse. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters. As you study examples and refactorings in this lesson, check which objectives you can demonstrate by writing a small interface and replacing conditionals with new implementations. Keep a mental note of one place in your codebase where this approach could reduce future edits.

This second objectives screen focuses on applying OCP in practice. You should be able to name a code example that violates OCP and describe precisely why it does so. For instance, a PaymentProcessor with many payment-type branches must be edited for each new method; that is a direct violation. You should also be able to list the steps to refactor such a class into an OCP-compliant design: extract an interface, create concrete implementations for each type, and let the processor depend on the abstraction. Another measurable skill is being able to weigh trade-offs: when is it appropriate to add a small interface for likely future changes, and when does an interface add unnecessary complexity? Finally, practice explaining why bug fixes are a permitted modification and how OCP is about adding new feature behavior via extension rather than forbidding all change. Use these objectives as checkboxes when you try the hands-on activity in this chapter.

Let's define the Open/Closed Principle in practical terms. The claim is simple: you should be able to add new functionality to a module without editing its existing, tested source code. That avoids introducing regressions into behavior you rely on. The apparent paradox — being both open and closed — is resolved when you separate what varies from what stays the same. The part that stays the same becomes closed or stable; the part that varies is represented by an abstraction that can be extended. For example, instead of a single class with many internal branches, define an interface that describes the operation you need. Then provide concrete implementations for each behavior. This way you add a new class when requirements change, rather than editing the original class. A common misconception is that OCP forbids all changes. It doesn't. Bug fixes and adjustments of the core are still modifications. OCP specifically guides how to add new behaviors without touching the proven core. Practically, this reduces regression risk, improves testability because each implementation can be tested in isolation, and makes the system easier to reason about. Think about one conditional you maintain often; could that be an interface with two or three implementations instead?

It's useful to separate the two halves of the principle and see their consequences. 'Open for extension' means you can add new behavior without changing the existing code base. This supports adding features by introducing new classes or modules that implement a common contract. 'Closed for modification' means once a component is established and tested, you minimize edits to its source to avoid regressions. Together they mean design for change rather than making change in place. Practically, open-for-extension encourages small, focused implementations: each new behavior is its own unit. Closed-for-modification pushes you to keep the core A P I stable and to let new behaviors plug in. A common mistake is to satisfy open-for-extension by duplicating or branching inside the same class, which violates closed-for-modification. Another misconception is to rigidly avoid refactoring; in reality, refactoring is how you achieve OCP — you extract abstractions and move behavior out. Consider this scenario: a reporting module grows formats. If you keep editing the big switch statement, you violate closed-for-modification. If instead you introduce a Report interface and add PDF, CSV, and Excel implementations, you stay closed to modification and open to extension. What would you extract first when you see a growing switch statement?

Let's examine a concrete code example that violates OCP and practice stating exactly why it does so. The PaymentProcessor class accepts a payment type string and uses an if-else cascade to choose behavior. Each time a new payment method arrives, you must open and edit the existing method to add another branch. That is changing working code to add new features, which increases regression risk. The code works for the current set of payment types, but it is brittle because every addition requires modification. A better design introduces a PaymentMethod abstraction that the processor depends on. Then new payment types are new classes implementing that abstraction and the processor simply calls a single method on the contract. A common misconception is that conditionals are harmless when small. They are harmless short-term, but once they grow and are edited repeatedly, they become maintenance hotspots. As you read the code, ask: who owns the decision logic? If the processor does, we violate OCP; if an injected strategy does, we comply. Consider how you would change the current class to add ApplePay. Would you edit the method or add a new class?

Refactoring a conditional hotspot into an OCP-compliant design is best done in small, verifiable steps. First, identify the smallest unit of varying behavior in your conditional. Second, extract an interface that captures that behavior with a single method name and clear inputs. Third, create concrete implementations for each existing branch and make sure their behavior matches current behavior. Fourth, update the original client to depend on the abstraction and accept implementations, for example by constructor injection or a registry lookup. Fifth, add tests for each implementation and for the client using a mock abstraction to ensure behavior remains unchanged. Finally, remove the old conditional only once tests confirm equivalence. Each step reduces risk: you never leave the system in an untested, broken state. A common misconception is that this must be done in a single big rewrite. Instead, move one branch at a time: extract one implementation, wire it in, test, then proceed. Following this incremental path keeps the codebase stable and makes code review simpler, because each change is small and focused.
